sections.overview: The northern fur seal is an eared seal of the North Pacific that spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore in dense colonies to breed. Most of the population breeds on the Pribilof Islands in the Bering Sea. Males are far larger than females.
sections.identification: It has a stocky body, a small head, a very short snout, small external ears and extremely dense fur. Its fore flippers are the longest of any eared seal. Adult males reach about 2 m and up to 270 kg and are dark brown to black,, while females are about 1.5 m, grey or brown above and paler below. Pups are born black and turn silver-grey after about three months.
sections.habitat: It breeds in the Bering Sea and along the eastern North Pacific, on islands such as St. Paul, St. George and Bogoslof in Alaska and on several Russian islands. Outside the breeding season it ranges widely over the North Pacific, the Bering Sea and the Sea of Okhotsk, and in winter reaches as far south as southern California and Honshu in Japan.
sections.diet: It is an opportunistic hunter of midwater fish and squid, and feeds mostly at night. Walleye pollock is the main prey over the Bering Sea shelf, while off the US West Coast it takes mackerel, squid, sardines and anchovies, among others.
sections.behavior: It is highly pelagic and mostly solitary at sea, and can stay out in the open ocean for nearly two years before returning to its breeding colonies. On land during the breeding season it is aggressive: males defend territories by pushing and biting, and fights between males can be fatal.
sections.reproduction: Males return to the breeding islands from May and hold territories, typically from about age 10. Females give birth to a single pup and mate again within about five days. Females usually have their first pup at 5–6 years and are most productive from about 8 to 13. Pups nurse until weaning at about four months.
sections.ecology: As a predator of schooling fish and squid, the northern fur seal links the open North Pacific to its breeding islands. It is itself preyed on by killer whales, Steller sea lions and sharks. Pups are taken by Steller sea lions, and entanglement in marine debris and lost fishing gear is a major hazard.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the species as Vulnerable (assessed in 2015). In the US it is protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, and the Pribilof Islands and Eastern Pacific stock was listed as depleted in 1988 after falling by more than half from about 2.2 million seals in the 1950s. Its 2019 abundance estimate was about 627,000, and pup production declined roughly 1.8% a year from 1999 to 2019.
